cultivar: Fu'an and Fuding Dabai and other downy Fujian cultivars; Yunnan large-leaf for Yunnan-sourced lots
processing: Fully oxidised tippy gongfu black: a bud with one leaf is withered, rolled so the leaf curls around the bud, oxidised and dried, then sorted to keep the golden tips.
harvest_season: Spring (April), from early pickings with plenty of bud; the name is a Western trade grade rather than a seasonal product.
appearance_dry: Curled, slightly hooked dark strands with golden tips that, with some imagination, look like little monkey paws.
appearance_liquor: Bright orange-red with a golden rim.
appearance_wet: Tender copper-red leaf with pale golden buds.
taste_profile: Honey and peach sweetness over soft cocoa, a creamy texture and a gentle finish with little tannin.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at around 90 °C, short steeps. Western-style, which is how it is usually sold: 3 g per 250 ml, 2.5–3 minutes, neat.

vintage_note: Sold by Western retailers as the current year's spring tea, rarely with a date, which is the thing to ask for; drink within a year. In China the same tea is sold as a tippy Tanyang or Bailin gongfu grade or as 'Jin Hao', so there is no Chinese vintage market under this name.
description:
Golden Monkey is a Western shop name rather than a Chinese one: it is what English-speaking retailers call a tippy, bud-and-leaf Fujian gongfu black whose curled golden tips supposedly resemble monkey paws. In China the same tea would be sold as a high grade of Tanyang or Bailin gongfu, or simply as 'jin hao' (golden tip) black from Fu'an or Fuding; some retailers also sell Yunnan tippy black under the name. It is on this list because it is one of the most common ways an English-speaking tea drinker meets Fujian black tea.

The tea itself is a well-made gongfu black: a bud with one leaf from downy Fujian cultivars, withered, rolled so the leaf wraps around the bud, oxidised and dried, then sorted for tips. The high bud content is what gives it the honeyed softness, and the Fujian cultivars give a peach-like fruit that Yunnan-sourced versions replace with malt.

In the cup expect honey and peach over soft cocoa, a creamy texture and very little tannin; it gives six or seven short steeps at around 90 °C and a friendly pot at three minutes. The mistake is to brew it strong and milky out of habit – it is a neat-drinking tea.

Because the name is a grade rather than an origin, buying well means asking what is behind it: which county, which spring, and how tippy. A good Golden Monkey has visible golden curls through dark leaf and a sweet, fruity dry aroma; a dull, flat, tipless leaf is a lower grade with a better name. Expect to pay more than for a plain Fujian gongfu and less than for Jin Jun Mei.

If you like it, go to the source: a Tanyang or Bailin gongfu bought under its own name from a Fujian seller is the same tea with a better paper trail.
sources_note: A Western trade name; the mapping to Tanyang/Bailin tippy grades is the usual trade explanation and the Chinese name 金猴茶 is a back-translation used by some sellers.
history:
Golden Monkey has no firm history behind it, because the name is used loosely. Reference entries warn that it can cover many black teas and advise judging the leaf rather than the label. Harney & Sons, an American tea company, places its lot in northern Fujian around Panyang, Zhenghe and Fu'an and names the Da Bai cultivar, which fits the usual trade explanation: a bud-heavy Fujian gongfu sold under a Western shop name. Other reference entries connect the name with Yunnan, so both origins are in circulation.

The name is said to come from leaves that look like monkey claws. Stories about local landlords, taipans and a tea about 300 years old circulate without any evidence behind them, and they are better treated as shop lore. The one concrete record is a second place in the Signature Famous Teas hot tea class at the 2009 World Tea Championship.
